normalized.governing_thought: Yes, raise prices in 2027, but target them: +10% for mid-market, up to contract caps for enterprise, and hold SMB until a renewal test proves it can bear an increase
executive_summary: Rising churn is a promotion problem, not a price problem
About 94% of the 1.1-pt rise in SMB monthly churn comes from the 2,100 customers acquired by the 2025 50%-off promotion; they churn ~4.9%/month
Elsewhere churn barely moved: non-promo SMB 2.0→2.1%, enterprise flat. 18% of non-promo churners cite price, vs 19% of all SMB churners in 2025
Onboarding will help but cannot halve SMB churn: even full activation gets it to ~2.0%, not 1.55%
There is headroom in mid-market and enterprise, but it is unproven in SMB
Mid-market: a +10% list test cut conversion by only 0.5 pts (not significant); NRR is 112%; Inkwell is not seen in deals above 200 seats
Enterprise: NRR 118%, churn 0.2%/month, but only 40% of ARR renews in 2027 and 60% is capped at +7%
SMB competes with Inkwell's $9 plan (win rate 51%→38%). An increase breaks even if churn reacts at ~2× the 2023 rate
A targeted increase carries far less risk than a blanket 12%, but no pricing option delivers 15% growth on its own
The proposed +12% on every plan is worth $7.6M gross, not $10.3M, because only part of the ARR renews and caps apply. Net of churn it is $1.5–4.6M, and it loses money on SMB in the stress case
The targeted plan nets $2.2–3.6M. Raising prices for the promotion cohort loses money even at the 2023 churn response
With the plan, ARR reaches $96.4–97.8M before new customers. Reaching $98.9M needs $1.1–2.5M of new-logo ARR. NRR stays at ~112–114%
Roll out in three gated stages, with triggers that would change the plan
January: reprice mid-market and enterprise renewals. Q1–Q2: randomised SMB renewal test. July: SMB go/no-go. Throughout: an activation programme for the promotion cohort
Watch mid-market renewal churn (>1.0%/month triggers a cap at +5%) and the SMB test arm. Define one board churn metric and get a 2027 new-logo plan

slides.title: We started from "raise mid-market and enterprise, freeze SMB"; the evidence backed most of it, rejected two internal claims, and changed our SMB answer

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis (week 1): raise prices for mid-market and enterprise, where customers stay for integrations and the audit trail; freeze SMB, because the churn rise looks like a promotion effect that a price rise would make worse.
1 The churn rise is concentrated in the promotion cohort, not the core base — Supported
evidence: Non-promo SMB 2.0→2.1%; promo cohort implied 4.9%; ~94% of the SMB rise comes from the cohort

claims.claim: 2 Core customers have not become more price-sensitive — Supported for retention; open for acquisition
evidence: Non-promo price citations 18% (vs 19% for all SMB in 2025)
SMB win rate against Inkwell fell 51%→38%

claims.claim: 3 Mid-market and enterprise can absorb ~10% at renewal — Largely supported (test covered new sign-ups only)
evidence: Test: −0.5 pt conversion (not significant); NRR 112%/118%; no Inkwell above 200 seats
Mid-market churn did rise 0.6→0.8%

claims.claim: 4 SMB cannot bear any increase — Not supported: answer changed to "test, then decide"
evidence: 2023 rise kept ~half its value; non-promo base stable → a freeze is too cautious, a blanket rise too risky

claims.claim: 5 The CFO's claim: 12% on all plans = $10.3M — Rejected
evidence: $7.6M gross; $1.5–4.6M net

claims.claim: 6 The Customer Success claim: onboarding halves SMB churn in two quarters — Rejected
evidence: ~2.8% if the cohort reaches normal activation; ~2.0% even if every customer activates; 1.55% is out of reach
low activators churn at 3× the rate

slides.title: The churn rise sits almost entirely in the 2,100 promotion customers; non-promo SMB churn moved only 0.1 pt

claims.claim: ~94% of the SMB increase is the promotion cohort
evidence: Monthly logo churn H1 2025 → H1 2026: SMB non-promo (3,800 cust.) 2 → 2.1; SMB promo cohort (2,100 cust.) — → 4.9; Mid-market (1,350 cust.) 0.6 → 0.8; Enterprise (150 cust.) 0.2 → 0.2
Promotion cohort: 36% of customers × (4.9% − 2.0%) = +1.04 pts
Non-promo drift: 64% of customers × (2.1% − 2.0%) = +0.06 pts
Total SMB rise +1.10 pts (2.0% → 3.1%)
Promo-cohort churn is implied: (5,900 × 3.1% − 3,800 × 2.1%) ÷ 2,100 = 4.9%

claims.claim: The cohort is 36% of SMB customers but ~56% of SMB churners
evidence: 103 of 183 a month
Its annualised churn is ~45%, against ~22% for other SMB customers

claims.claim: Mid-market churn did rise from 0.6% to 0.8% (≈7% to 9% a year). The pack gives no cause; we treat it as a watch item
The board dashboard's "1.4% → 2.3%" does not reconcile with these figures (see A2).

slides.title: Promotion customers leave when the discount ends and rarely set the product up; the rest of the base is no more price-sensitive than in 2025

claims.claim: Three signs this is about acquisition quality, not list price
evidence: Share of churners citing price: All SMB H1 2025 19; All SMB H1 2026 34; Non-promo SMB H1 2026 18; Promo cohort H1 2026 52
41% vs 72%: share of new customers sending ≥5 documents in month 1: promo cohort vs other cohorts
~3×: churn rate of SMB customers sending <5 documents in month 1, vs those sending more
≤2 months: after the 50% discount ended, most promo churners had left
18% vs 19%: non-promo SMB churners citing price, H1 2026 vs all SMB H1 2025: no new price sensitivity in retention

claims.claim: To them the "price" reason is a doubling of their bill, not the list price

the CFO is right that the churn rise is not about the list price, and the CEO is right that the promotion cohort is fragile. A list increase applied to the cohort would hit the group that already cites price 2.9× as often
the survey slightly under-weights the cohort
evidence: A blended 34% implies ~47% of respondents were promo churners, below their ~56% share of churners

slides.title: An activation programme is worth running but cannot halve SMB churn: lifting the cohort to normal activation cuts SMB churn from 3.1% to ~2.8%, not 1.55%

claims.claim: Lifting the cohort to normal activation cuts SMB churn from 3.1% to ~2.8%
evidence: Churn of an activated SMB customer: 2.1% ÷ (72% × 1 + 28% × 3) = 1.35%
Churn of a low-activation customer: 3 × 1.35% = 4.04%
Cohort churn explained by its 41% activation: 1.35% × (41% + 59% × 3) = 2.93%
Excess not explained (discount cliff, low intent): 4.91% − 2.93% = 1.97%
Cohort churn if activation reaches 72%: 4.91% − (2.93% − 2.10%) = 4.07%
SMB churn after the programme: (3,800 × 2.1% + 2,100 × 4.07%) ÷ 5,900 = 2.8%
Upper bound: every SMB customer activated: 2.0%

claims.claim: Halving to 1.55% is not credible
evidence: It would put SMB below its pre-promotion level (2.0%) and below the pre-increase level in 2023 (1.8%). Even the upper bound only reaches ~2.0%.

claims.claim: 2027 ARR effect is small
evidence: about $0.27M if the cohort reaches normal activation from January. We include $0.2M on the assumption the programme partly succeeds.

claims.claim: The bigger value is prevention. Future acquisition offers should reward set-up (for example, documents sent), not just sign-up.
evidence: 41% activation and ~45% annual churn

claims.claim: Price policy for the cohort: hold at the current full price through 2027
evidence: The cohort cites price 2.9× as often as other churners, so a 12% rise on it loses money even at the 2023 churn response (slide 9)

slides.title: Mid-market and enterprise can carry an increase: low churn, NRR above 110%, a price test with no significant loss, and no low-cost rival in large deals

claims.claim: Headroom verdict: SMB Unproven: test first; Mid-market Yes: +10% (the tested level); Enterprise Yes: up to the cap
evidence: ARR / customers: SMB $21.0M / 5,900; Mid-market $41.0M / 1,350; Enterprise $24.0M / 150
Monthly logo churn H1 2026: SMB 3.1% (≈31%), non-promo 2.1% (≈22%); Mid-market 0.8% (≈9%), up from 0.6%; Enterprise 0.2% (≈2%)
NRR trailing 12 months: SMB 94%; Mid-market 112%; Enterprise 118%
SMB: 2023 +8%: churn spiked 1.8→2.3% for 6 months, then settled at 1.9%
Mid-market: 2024 +10% for new sign-ups: conversion 23.1% vs 23.6% (n.s.); revenue per lead +7.7%
Enterprise: None direct; increases capped at 7% on 60% of ARR
SMB: Inkwell $9 vs Palisade $15; win rate 51%→38% where Inkwell is considered
Mid-market: Integrations and audit trail (customer advisory board); Inkwell not seen above 200 seats
Enterprise: Same reasons; Inkwell not seen
ARR that renews in 2027: SMB 100% ($21.0M); Mid-market 85% ($34.9M); Enterprise 40% ($9.6M)

claims.claim: Caveats: the 2024 test covered new sign-ups, not renewals, and mid-market churn did rise 0.2 pts. Inkwell may reach smaller mid-market deals (≤200 seats).

slides.title: In SMB, an increase pays only if churn reacts at less than ~2× its 2023 response, and Inkwell makes that uncertain: test before committing

claims.claim: Net 2027 ARR from +8% on non-promo SMB renewals depends on churn response
For an increase: the 2023 +8% kept about half its value in year one
evidence: Non-promo churn (2.0→2.1%) and price citations (19%→18%) barely moved from H1 2025 to H1 2026, despite Inkwell's Oct 2025 launch

claims.claim: Against: Inkwell Starter costs $9 vs Palisade SMB at $15
evidence: A 12% rise widens the gap from 67% to 87%
SMB win rate where Inkwell is considered has already fallen from 51% to 38%

claims.claim: Break-even: +8% stops paying if churn reacts at more than 2.1× the 2023 response (+12%: 2.0×)
evidence: Best case is +$0.7M, which is small against a $16.6M base

claims.claim: The promotion cohort fails even at 1×
evidence: its 2.9× higher price sensitivity turns +12% on $4.4M into -0.24M

claims.claim: Our call: run a randomised +8% test on non-promo renewals in Q1–Q2 and keep the new-customer list price at $15. Roll out from July only if churn stays within the 2023 pattern.
evidence: This gives up ~$0.3M of best-case upside to cap the downside

Non-promo SMB ARR = $21.0M − $4.4M = $16.6M

slides.title: Roll out in three stages with explicit go/no-go gates, so each step is backed by evidence from the one before

claims.claim: Mid-market & enterprise: Approve +10% / cap policy; brief CS and account teams; renewal notices (90 days) (Dec 2026); Reprice renewals from 1 Jan; track renewal rate weekly (Q1); Gate 1: renewal churn ≤ 1.0%/month and NRR on track → continue (Q2); Continue; prepare 2028 enterprise renewals (60% of ARR) (H2)

SMB non-promo: Design randomised test: +8% vs control on renewals; new-customer list stays $15; Test live; read early churn and exit reasons monthly; Gate 2 (end June): extra churn ≤ 0.5 pt (2023 pattern) → go; If go: +8% on all renewals from July. If no-go: stop; keep the test arm
evidence: The SMB test arms are ~1,900 non-promo customers each. Over six months a 0.5-pt monthly churn difference (≈240 vs ≈300 churners) is detectable at roughly 95% confidence.

slides.title: We ask leadership for five decisions in December; together they are worth $2.2–3.6M of net ARR and protect SMB while the evidence comes in

slides.title: How the option values are calculated: price uplift on 2027 renewing ARR minus the churn the price rise triggers

claims.claim: Model parameters
evidence: Renewing ARR in 2027: SMB 100% ($21.0M); MM 85% ($34.9M); Ent 40% ($9.6M) — Pack §8
Enterprise caps: 60% of renewing Ent ARR limited to +7% — assumes caps are spread evenly across renewal years
Gross uplift: Renewing ARR × price % — e.g. MM 34.85 × 10% = $3.49M
Price-driven churn: Renewing ARR × (1 + price) × k × price pts — Lost ARR measured at the new price
k, SMB non-promo: 0.45% per pt (base); 0.90% (stress, 2×) — 2023: (0.5 × 6 + 0.1 × 6) ÷ 8; stress reflects Inkwell
k, SMB promo cohort: 1.30% per pt (base); 2.60% (stress) — 2.9× non-promo, from price citations of 52% vs 18%
k, mid-market & enterprise: 0.21% per pt (base); 0.45% (stress) — 2024 test: 1 − 23.1/23.6 = 2.1% per 10 pts; stress uses SMB 2023
SMB gated rollout coverage: 50% of non-promo ARR repriced by year end (go); 25% (no-go)
Baseline existing-base ARR: $93.98M = 21.0 × 94% + 41.0 × 112% + 24.0 × 118% — Trailing NRR assumed to hold
Activation programme: +$0.2M (model maximum $0.27M) — Cohort churn 4.91% → 4.07% over 12 months on $4.4M

claims.claim: Simplification: uplift is applied to mid-2026 renewing ARR without netting out baseline churn (overstates SMB by up to ~6%).

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Existing mid-market customers react at renewal as mildly as new sign-ups did in the 2024 test (evidence quality Medium: test was new sign-ups; MM churn rose 0.6→0.8%); mid-market is ~75% of the plan's value
Non-promo SMB sensitivity is near the 2023 level despite Inkwell (evidence quality Low: precedent pre-dates Inkwell)
Trailing NRR (109%) holds in 2027 without a price change (Medium: trailing 12 months only); each 1 pt of NRR = $0.86M
New-logo ARR of at least $1.1–2.5M is achievable (Unknown: not in the pack)
Promo cohort keeps churning near 4.9% (or falls as the cliff passes) (Medium)

Assumes the 3× churn ratio for low activators (<5 documents in month 1) applies across the base, and that the cohort's activation gap explains part of its excess churn; the rest is treated as the effect of the discount ending
Stress case: SMB response 2× the 2023 level; mid-market and enterprise respond like SMB in 2023
Enterprise caps assumed spread evenly across renewal years (±$0.1M on the enterprise value)
One price % applied per segment; not split by SMB plan vs Business plan
Promo cohort ARR 'at full price' treated as current ARR ($4.4M of the $21.0M)
Simplification: uplift is applied to mid-2026 renewing ARR without netting out baseline churn (overstates SMB by up to ~6%)
Mid-market churn rise 0.6%→0.8% has no cause in the pack; treated as a watch item
Inkwell may reach smaller mid-market deals (≤200 seats)
Exit survey slightly under-weights the promo cohort
Board dashboard churn '1.4% → 2.3%' cannot be reproduced from segment data
All figures from the briefing pack are synthetic benchmark data; prepared without access to the decision owner for clarification
next_steps: Dec 2026: Approve +10% / cap policy; brief CS and account teams; send renewal notices (90 days)
Q1 2027: Reprice mid-market and enterprise renewals from 1 Jan; track renewal rate weekly
Q2 2027: Gate 1: renewal churn ≤ 1.0%/month and NRR on track → continue; otherwise cap at +5% for remaining renewals
H2 2027: Prepare 2028 enterprise renewals (60% of ARR)
Dec 2026: Design randomised SMB test: +8% vs control on renewals; new-customer list stays $15
Q1–Q2 2027: SMB test live; read early churn and exit reasons monthly
End June 2027: Gate 2: extra churn ≤ 0.5 pt → go; if go, +8% on all SMB renewals from July; if no-go, stop and keep the test arm
Promo cohort: freeze price; launch activation programme; track documents sent; measure activation lift vs 41% baseline; review whether the cohort joins the 2028 price plan
Define the board churn metric; report logo churn by segment and acquisition cohort plus gross revenue churn, with written definitions
Build a monthly pricing dashboard by segment and cohort
Track Inkwell win rate (SMB and MM ≤200 seats)
Year-end review of elasticity for the 2028 plan
Request/commission the 2027 new-logo ARR plan before the December decision
Stop deep, activation-blind acquisition discounts; tie future offers to set-up milestones (≥5 documents in month 1)
Size a separate SMB response to Inkwell (out of scope)
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck had no images, so there was nothing to transcribe from pictures. On slides 9 and 11 the waterfall charts came through as invisible 'base' series stacked under 'value' series. I recorded the visible step values, adding signs for the decreases based on the bridge logic. Slide 11's chart axis starts at $80M, so its absolute values (6, 17.80, 18.9) sit above that axis base. The 'Mid-market' entry on slide 11 is labelled in the chart as 'Mid-market +10%'. Some numbered labels on slides 2 and 15 (1–5) were out of order in the extraction; I reassembled the slide 15 decisions in numbered order. On slide 5, I paired the stat callouts (41% vs 72%, ~3×, ≤2 months, 18% vs 19%) with their descriptions by position in the text.
